speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Subsequently, I will move the second Motion separately, in compliance with Parliamentary procedural requirements.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: To carry out this important function, the IMF relies on resources provided by member countries, including Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This has allowed the IMF to respond to external shocks, including the COVID-19 pandemic and the war in Ukraine, by stepping up financing support to member countries.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The IMF has been stepping up its financial support for member countries to build resilience in an increasingly fragmented and fragile external environment.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Notably, it made the largest SDR allocation of US$650 billion to its member countries in 2021.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This SDR allocation was made to enable all members to address the long-term global need for reserves, build confidence and foster resilience of the international economy through a series of disruptive events.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As required under the IMF's Articles of Agreement, the US$650 billion SDR general allocation was distributed in proportion to the quota shares of IMF's members and not according to the relative needs of its members.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Singapore received 3.73 billion in SDR, notwithstanding that we did not require an augmentation of our resources.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The IMF is now calling on members with strong economic fundamentals and ample official foreign reserves to channel some of their SDR to various IMF trusts and programmes to support more vulnerable IMF members.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The amounts that Singapore has been asked to contribute are in line with Singapore's quota share at the IMF and a relatively small portion of the 3.7 billion SDR we received from the IMF in 2021.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Singapore will also be providing these contributions as part of broader, multilateral effort to support IMF's capacity to assist vulnerable, low-income countries.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: First, the IMF requests Singapore to assist in support of a fund programme for the benefit of one or more countries.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The PRGT and PRG-HIPC Trust are such fund programmes.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Second, at least one other member country has provided or intends to provide similar financial assistance.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This condition has been fulfilled, with a good representation of member countries pledging support or already contributing to the two programmes.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Third, MAS publicly discloses key information about the financial assistance via a Gazette publication.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Fourth, Parliament fixes by resolution the maximum amount of the grants.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I will now explain the specific context and considerations for the two grants.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: First, Singapore's grant contribution to the Poverty Reduction and Growth Trust (PRGT).

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The PRGT supports the IMF's concessional lending to low-income countries.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It plays a central role in debt resolution for distressed countries and provided emergency support to many low-income countries during the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The IMF's annual lending commitments increased five-fold compared to the pre-pandemic period to 5.5 billion SDR per annum during 2020 to 2023.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This surge in lending during the pandemic, coupled with the sustained high financing needs post-pandemic, driven by tighter financial conditions and rising food prices, have placed significant strain on the PRGT's finances.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The IMF is hence seeking voluntary contributions from economically stronger member countries to support the PRGT's longer-term financial sustainability.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The quantum of our proposed contribution to the PRGT is commensurate with our quota share at the IMF, which stands at 0.82% today.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Next, Singapore's grant contribution to the PRG-HIPC Trust to support Sudan's debt relief.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The IMF and World Bank launched the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) Initiative in 1996.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It is to ensure that no poor country faces an unmanageable debt burden.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: To be eligible for the HIPC Initiative, countries need to meet certain criteria and also to commit to policy changes to reduce poverty, and then demonstrate a record of doing so.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In 2005, the HIPC Initiative was supplemented by the Multilateral Debt Relief Initiative.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This allows countries to receive 100% relief on eligible debts by the IMF, the World Bank and the African Development Fund after demonstrating sustained economic performance, implementing key structural and social reforms and also maintaining macroeconomic stability.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: IMF financing for the HIPC Initiative comes from bilateral contributions from members and IMF resources, mainly investment income on proceeds from the IMF's gold sales in 1999.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: However, resources in the PRG-HIPC Trust have been insufficient to finance debt relief to the remaining two HIPC countries with protracted arrears to the IMF – that is, Somalia and Sudan.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The IMF has thus initiated separate fundraising efforts to mobilise the resources needed for it to cover its share of debt relief to Somalia and Sudan.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: There has been no request for further contribution to Somalia.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Sudan is amongst the world's poorest countries, with an estimated two thirds of its population living in poverty.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Its history is marked by political instability, internal conflict and isolation from the world economy.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Following Sudan's efforts to re-engage with the international community in 2020, it met the necessary conditions to begin receiving debt relief under the HIPC Initiative.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Completing this process would allow Sudan to regain debt sustainability and help it implement essential reforms to free up resources to tackle poverty and improve the social conditions for its people.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The quantum of our contribution is determined based on our quota share at the IMF.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Similar to the PRGT, Singapore’s contribution towards the debt relief for Sudan is part of a broader multilateral effort, with 122 members also having pledged to contribute, including our ASEAN-4 neighbours: Indonesia, Malaysia, Philippines and Thailand.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Why should Singapore make these contributions to the IMF, considering today’s uncertain global environment?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: With multilateralism under threat, we should support multilateral institutions such as the IMF to help them to play their role in maintaining the stability of the global system.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It is also in Singapore’s interest to do so, because we are a stakeholder in the international community and it is our role to support the IMF.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As a small open economy with multiple connections to global markets, Singapore has an interest in supporting initiatives that promote global resilience to crises and to safeguard stability in the global monetary system.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Singapore also joins a broader base of other countries in supporting IMF programmes.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As noted earlier, Singapore’s OFR increased by 3.73 billion SDR following IMF’s 2021 SDR allocation.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The proposed grant amounts are also proportionate to Singapore’s quota share at the IMF and are consistent with Singapore’s standing in the international financial system.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Following Parliament’s resolution to fix the maximum amount of grants that MAS can allocate to the IMF’s PRGT and PRG-HIPC Trust, MAS will publish in the Gazette key information about the grants.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our GPC Members for Finance, and Trade and Industry – Member Victor Lye, Shaun Loh, Ng Shi Xuan and Lee Hong Chuang – come from varied backgrounds including finance and investments, local business and industry.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We will be sharing our concerns and clarifications as well as some suggestions on these two Motions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Victor Lye will touch on global stability, prudence and Singapore’s national interest.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Member Ng Shi Xuan will focus on careful examination of safeguards, proportionality and accountability in Singapore’s IMF contributions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Lee Hong Chuang aims to provide a strategic, values-based case for multilateral engagement grounded in Singapore’s economic interests.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Member Shawn Loh will touch on the longer-term picture of multilateral institutions like the IMF and asking what our strategy would be.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Singapore has always affirmed that contributing as a responsible member of the international community is in our national interest.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Having once been a beneficiary of World Bank financing that supported our early infrastructure development between 1963 and 1975, we recognise that promoting stability, growth and debt sustainability in lower-income and vulnerable economies contributes to a more resilient global system, one that ultimately benefits a small and open economy like Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, I do have some clarifications and suggestions, which I would put in three main buckets.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, I wonder how much our world view has evolved, or needs to evolve, amidst the changing world order that we see today.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The IMF is founded upon the United Nations and Bretton Woods system which has underpinned international economic relations for decades since World War II.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On that basis, I am aligned with Minister Ong Ye Kung’s statement when we moved similar Motions in this House back in 2021, that “it is in Singapore's interest to be part of this international community where we work together, where we cooperate, where there are rules, there are norms, there are best practices that hold every country into account to ensure that we live peacefully together in a global village”.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, today we see that old multilateral world order is under threat, if not already consigned to history.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many countries are turning protectionist and focusing on narrow conceptions of national interest.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, the question I have is, do Minister Ong’s words in 2021 still hold true?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Do they still justify our continued contribution of significant amounts to uplift other countries in need?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One of the safeguards that Parliament had implemented on our loans and grants to the IMF is that our contribution must be part of a multilateral effort.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the latest round of collective fundraising for the PRGT and for supporting Sudan’s debt relief efforts, how many countries are joining the efforts and who are they?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The increasing fragmentation of the global world order also poses interesting questions for us.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Just recently, we have seen news that the US has invited Singapore to join its “Board of Peace” to supervise the next phase of the Gaza peace plan.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Commentators have observed that Gaza may just be a pretext for setting up a corporate version of the United Nations, where countries may buy themselves a permanent seat at the table for US$1 billion payable in case within the first year.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How will we decide which organisations and international development efforts going forward to support as well?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This applies especially when Singapore is asked to contribute monetary resources, in addition to the other specialised capacity building programmes that we run for government officials, representatives of non-governmental organisations (NGOs) and other organisations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Enhanced Technical Assistance Package for the Palestinian Authority is one example of the latter programmes that Singapore provides and has been useful.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When countries including Singapore made a round of pledges to the IMF’s PRGT back in 2012, the IMF estimated that these additional resources would be able to sustain the PRGT lending to impoverished countries for two decades.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Yet, today we need another injection into the PRGT.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would the PRGT eventually reach an amount that is self-sustaining, or will continual injections be required?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In a 2024 IMF policy paper, one of the reasons given for the fundraising need is that there has been a post-COVID-19 surge in requests and demand for financial assistance by countries.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Or do we expect this to set a new norm for the level of financial assistance expected by developing countries?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Does our support translate into enhanced participation or influence in IMF committees, programme design, or technical assistance priorities?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am aware that Minister of State Alvin Tan has shared some parts of it earlier, but please indulge me in some questions on this front.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, can the Minister of State clarify whether these grants are funded from MAS’ investment income or operating surpluses, and I think Minister of State Alvin Tan has mentioned that they do involve some direct draw, may not involve draw from Singapore’s OFR.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This may need further clarification from Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These clarifications would help assure Singaporeans and Members of this House that while we remain a responsible global citizen, we continue to exercise prudence and discipline in managing our national resources.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Third, Mr Deputy Speaker, we must heighten awareness among Singaporeans of our international assistance efforts – what we are doing, why do we do it and how are we doing it.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is especially since not many people would read the Government Gazette, where the Government is required to publish the key information of the assistance provided to the IMF under our Bretton Woods Agreements Act.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Getting our citizens’ buy-in is important because there may be sentiments that we should help ourselves before helping others.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In many other countries, this bitterness at “what could have been” has led to the rise of far-right movements and politics.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These ideologies, which encompass xenophobia and identity politics, are deeply divisive and have triggered violence many a times.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In this regard, I have a few suggestions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One, can we give more weight to the role of these international organisations and Singapore’s relationship with them in our national education syllabus?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Speaking to Singaporeans today, some of them are surprised or unaware that Singapore had actually been a huge beneficiary of World Bank assistance when we were building from Third World to First.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, we can celebrate these organisations and the work they do in more public roadshows or commemorative events.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is especially since we host many of these international organisations in Singapore, such as the IMF-Singapore Regional Training Institute and the IMF Resident Representative Office.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But beyond contributing financial resources in a prudent manner, we should also consider how Singaporeans can participate in the development and implementation of international assistance programmes on the ground.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: More and more Singaporeans are in fact interested in making a real difference to our world, as exemplified by Singapore charity Rahmatan Lil Alamin Foundation’s efforts for Gaza.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I declare, however, that while I maintain personal and professional relationships with staff at the World Bank, as well as a small balance in its retirement fund, I have no ongoing financial interests in the institution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This speech is therefore delivered in my capacity as a Singaporean Parliamentarian.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The fund has been engaged in poverty reduction work for several decades now, and while I personally find that this smacks of mission creep, especially relative to its mandate versus the World Bank, I will concede that helping one of the poorest nations on earth need not be limited to the actions of one international agency alone.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In previous Motions of this nature, I had argued in favour of transferring some of our additional surplus quota contributions to other countries that are in need, and this Motion is precisely along those lines.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: First, I will seek more clarity on the choice of parameters for support; econd, I hope to obtain some additional context for the historical disbursements to the PRGT; and third, I will return to my call for a more institutionalised system for our nation's foreign assistance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My first clarification has to do with the $36 million and $8 million sort.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As Minister of State Tan shared, the amount for the PRGT contribution was conveyed by the IMF and as is typical, is consistent with our nation's quota subscription at the institution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The amount for Sudan, under the auspices of the HIPC Initiative, is also presumably a proportional contribution to the total amount of debt relief that the country seeks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Still, I wish to ascertain that this is indeed how these specific amounts will arrive there.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Second, I have no doubt that Sudan is in severe need for debt relief, with a gross domestic product (GDP) per capita of about $1,250, the country is one of the poorest worldwide.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The nation is faced with a debt of close to 2.5 times its annual income and recent analyses strongly suggest that this amount is unsustainable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Still, there are 39 countries listed on the HIPC list.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This includes countries that are poorer, such as Afghanistan, Burundi, Malawi, as well as those with equally crushing debt burdens, such as Eritrea.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And while all but two countries on the HIPC list have previously enjoyed that relief, Eritrea, like Sudan, have not.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I would therefore like to understand the premise behind the selection of Sudan as the beneficiary of this round of relief.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, this may well have been recommended by the staff of the Fund, but as donors, I believe that it is incumbent on us to also question the institution's rationale.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am also aware that the amounts constitute maximums, which in principle, may turn out not to be fully assessed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, it is uncertain whether this amount has been fully disbursed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Relatedly, how do the current grants relate to our earlier commitments?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, $36 million is a minuscule share, just about 3% of the prior $1.25 billion pledge.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Why not simply tap on the earlier pool if it has not been paid out in full?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Or are the two buckets materially different, insofar as the $1.25 billion was a pledge that could be called on, whereas the present monies are grants that will, for sure, be tapped?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The step would not even entail that much of a budgetary impact.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This would simply collect our routine IMF and International Development Association subscriptions but also include a modest budget for a development fund to extend ad hoc aid, especially in the wake of economic crises or natural disasters.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To avoid frivolous disbursements, we can roll over annual budget subscriptions that remain unspent with no stipulation to exhaust funds in any given year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such a move would step away from arbitrary allocations and idiosyncratic motions, and subject such funding to our standard, and in my view, more professional budget scrutiny mechanisms, such as the Public Accounts Committee and the annual report of the Auditor-General.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, I support both Motions before the House, relating to grants to the IMF's PRGT and the trust supporting Sudan's debt relief.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: My remarks focus on how these grants are controlled and what Singapore expects in return.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Unlike some IMF arrangements that involve lending or reserve assets, these two Motions involve grants, which are not repaid.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: But it is still important to be clear that these are direct transfers of public funds, not investments or loans.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Can the Government clarify whether grants of this nature are expected to be occasional and case-specific, or whether they are likely to become regular or automatic over time?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: And what principles are used to keep them limited in size and scope?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Second, on whether Singapore is doing more than its fair share.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: We understand that these grants sit outside domestic spending and do not reduce what Ministries receive through the Budget.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Despite this narrative, as Minister of State Tan has shared, many countries are still contributing to these IMF trusts.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: That suggests countries still see value in doing so.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: But the question is whether Singapore's share is reasonable.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Third, on what changes on the ground and how this is monitored.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: For the PRGT, and especially for Sudan's debt relief, Singaporeans will want to know what these grants are meant to achieve and whether there are adequate safeguards governing their use.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Sudan does not have strong institutions and is embroiled in ongoing conflict.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Debt relief may be necessary, but it also carries risks if money is not used properly.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Does the governance structure ensure that the money is used where it is most needed?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: And will contributors receive updates on how the funds are used and what outcomes are achieved?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Fourth, on flexibility if Singapore's own budgets come under pressure.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: While these grants are modest, they are still public funds.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: It is therefore reasonable to ask what flexibility Singapore has, if fiscal conditions tighten in the future.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: If Singapore faces tighter budgets, what options do we have to pause, reduce or recover overseas commitments, whether in the form of grants or loans, and how are these decisions made?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I will begin my speech in Mandarin, followed by English.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: There is a great philosopher Mencius who once said, "大舍前,齐天下".

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: What it means is, "When successful, help the whole world." It means that once you have strength or prosperity, you should assist others.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The underlying philosophy is that prosperity should lead to long-term stability, including for oneself.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: At its core, this motion is not merely about an overseas financial commitment.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It is about the kind of global partner Singapore chooses to be in an increasingly uncertain and volatile world.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: On the surface, this is resource support; at a deeper level, it reflects how we view risks, and how Singapore positions itself in an uncertain environment.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I believe that supporting the PRGT is sound in principle, necessary in overall assessment, restrained and measured in the use of public funds and aligns with Singapore's long-standing position of supporting multilateral systems and international cooperation.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Our prosperity depends on global stability, open trade and a resilient international financial system.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: When low-income countries are hit by shocks, whether from pandemics, climate events, debt distress or conflict, the effects do not remain local.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They spill across borders through disrupted supply chains, financial volatility and regional instability.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: These risks can come fast, ultimately affecting jobs, investment and confidence here in Singapore, especially for SMEs.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This helps countries stabilise their macroeconomic conditions, protect essential social spending and undertake necessary reforms, preventing local crises from escalating into systemic ones.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Seen this way, support for the PRGT is not simply aid; it is a form of early risk prevention.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The answer lies in the strength of the mechanism.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: IMF programmes are grounded in rigorous assessment, clear policy conditions and strong monitoring, ensuring that funds are used to restore stability and confidence.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Meanwhile, IMF also has ability to mobilise resources quickly and coordinate internationally, an essential capability during cross-border crises.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In addressing international balance of payments and financial crises, IMF's expertise enables relevant arrangement can be implemented under stress.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The concessional nature of the PRGT allows low-income countries to stabilise their economies without sacrificing people's basic needs.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As a small state, we understand the value of clear rules.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They make things predictable and allow small nations to have space and sense of security in the system.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Our approach to international cooperation has always emphasised effectiveness, responsibility and systemic impact.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Of course, we must also address domestic concerns.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It is understandable that some Singaporeans may ask why we should support efforts overseas when there are domestic needs.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: There are three points I would like to mention.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Second, this is not a zero-sum choice, external stability directly supports Singapore's economic resilience, investment and employment.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Third, our own experience shows that external shocks can spread rapidly.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Helping others stabilise their economies reduces the spillover risks that could otherwise reach our shores.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Without concessional financing, they may be forced into sharp cuts to essential services or disorderly defaults, creating broader financial and social instability.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The PRGT is a vital tool to prevent such outcomes and to safeguard international financial stability by helping countries to stabilise their fundamentals at the most difficult times.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, in English, please.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: At its core, this Motion is not merely about an overseas financial commitment.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It is about the kind of global partners Singapore choose to be in an increasingly uncertain and volatile world.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Our prosperity depends on global stability, open trade and a resilient international financial system.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: When low-income countries are hit by shocks, whether from pandemic climate events, debt distress or conflict, the effects do not remain local.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They spill across borders through disrupted supply chain, financial volatility and regional instability.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: These risks ultimately affect jobs, investment and confidence here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The PRGT plays a critical role by providing timely and concessional financing to vulnerable economics at the onset of crisis.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This helps countries stabilise their macroeconomics condition, protect essential social spending and undertaking necessary reforms, preventing local crisis from escalating into systematic ones.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Seen this way, support from the PRGT is not simply about aid.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It is a form of early risk prevention.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The answer lies in the strength of the mechanism.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: IMF programmes are grounded in rigorous assessment, clear policy conditions and strong monitoring, ensuring that funds are used to restore stability and confidence.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The IMF also has the expertise and ability to mobilise resources quickly and coordinate internationally, and essential capability during cross-border crisis.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Importantly, the concessional nature of the PRGT allowed low-income countries to stabilise their economics without sacrificing basic healthcare, education or social needs.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Supporting the PRGT is also consistent with Singapore's long-standing commitment to a rules-based multilateral system.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As a small state, we understand the value of clear rules, accountability and predictable frameworks.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Our approach to international cooperation has always emphasised effectiveness, responsibility and systematic impact.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It is understandable that some Singaporeans may ask why we should support efforts overseas when there are domestic needs.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: There are three points I would like to mention here.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: External stability directly supports Singapore's economic resiliency and employment.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Third, our own experience show that external shocks can spread rapidly.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Helping others stabilise their economy reduces the spillover risks that could otherwise reach our shores.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The PGRT is a vital tool to prevent such outcomes and to safeguard international financial stability.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Only through shared development that lasting prosperity can be achieved.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Lee, I hope you will get back your voice very soon.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Singapore has long benefited from today’s global order, which was built on multilateral institutions, such as the United Nations, the World Bank and the IMF.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: It is this global order that has pretty much allowed us to earn our living in the world.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Our externally oriented economy can grow faster, and Singaporeans can access opportunities better, when global trade and financial flows increase and when more of such global flows flow through Singapore.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: This takes place when there are clear rules that countries abide by.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: It also takes place when more countries around the world experience economic development, financial stability and are plugged into the global economy.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: It is therefore in our national interest to ensure that the global economic environment remains conducive for Singapore to earn our good living, way into the future.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: For now, these multilateral institutions help us to do so.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: As responsible members of the global community, we have been contributing our fair share.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I would, however, like to raise three points.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: First, can the Government track where Singapore’s contributions are used so that we can find ways to deepen economic relations with these countries?

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: This would help both sides enjoy economically stable, win-win relations.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Coincidentally, it is equivalent to around US$1 billion, the same fee to have a long-term seat on the US’ Board of Peace, although the contribution to IMF’s trust would be a loan, whereas the Board of Peace requires an expense.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: As a loan, it remains as an asset on MAS’ balance sheet.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Can the Government share more about the mechanism of this loan to the IMF and whether there are any risks from this loan?

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I am not so sure compared to my other Parliamentary colleagues: what should Singapore’s long-term strategy be, given the emergence of a more fragmented world order, divided into more adversarial blocs and driven by self-interest among states?

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: We have seen this in the Non-Aligned Movement of the 1950s, the formation of BRICS in the 2000s and so on.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: But in most instances in the past, these blocs were combinations of developing countries and middle powers, attempting to challenge incumbent multilateral institutions and an order underpinned by developed countries, first and foremost among them, the US.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: The challenger is not another bloc of developing countries.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: It is the US itself, rebalancing its interests vis-à-vis these multilateral institutions.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: We should therefore expect institutions like the IMF to come under extreme stress.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Perhaps, they will even be unable to perform the key, international functions they were set up to do, such as development support or liquidity in times of global crises.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Some of our colleagues in the House have assumed that they will continue to do so in the future.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: What if some member countries refuse to honour their obligations to supply their currencies as required by the Special Drawing Rights?

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: How should we respond to these new developments based on our own national interest?

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Should we capitalise on the opportunity to take a larger role in re-shaping existing multilateral institutions?

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Or should we capitulate and follow the herd of other countries looking out for their own immediate self-interest, potentially re-organising into new blocs?

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: But I thought to leave these questions as food for thought.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Because as the old adage goes, if we do not have a seat at the table, then we might find ourselves on the menu.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The key point is that, to many Singaporeans, these may sound very foreign and very distant.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But they are indeed relevant to us because Singapore is a small, open economy, deeply connected to the global trade, to global markets and global supply chains.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The key point is that when fragile economies collapse, the impact does not remain overseas.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such shocks and financial crises can quickly affect prices, jobs and business confidence in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Therefore, supporting these IMF trust funds is a form of reducing the likelihood of global shocks that would otherwise raise costs for households and businesses in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That said, I recognise that Singaporeans may have concerns.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That they are funded from current resources and that no Reserves are being touched.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That they are budgeted expenditures alongside and do not compete with our domestic priorities.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For a highly trade-dependent economy like ours, supporting global financial stability is a matter of national economic interest.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At a time when commitment to multilateral rules is understrained globally, supporting well-governed institutions like the IMF is especially important for small states that rely on predictability rather than power.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, for these reasons and with the clarifications I have stated, I support the Motions.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Members have highlighted the importance for Singapore to contribute to the IMF and to help other vulnerable economies, especially in today’s volatile and fragmented global environment.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: First, they have asked whether Singapore should continue contributing to the international community in the current global environment.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Mr Shawn Loh asked about Singapore's strategy in a more fragmented world and our interests as part of the global and international community.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We do indeed face a very different global operating context today, with multilateralism under threat amid wars, rising protectionism and intensifying geopolitical tensions.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Prime Minister Wong had emphasised that even as multilateralism comes under threat, Singapore must do our part to preserve multilateral frameworks that matter and to lay the foundation for a more stable global order to emerge in the years ahead.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Lee Hong Chuang put it well: this Motion concerns not just a financial commitment.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It is about the kind of global partner Singapore chooses to be.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And it is against this backdrop that Singapore must and will continue to support key multilateral institutions, such as the IMF.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As a small city-state with an open economy and a global financial centre, Singapore has a strong interest in the continued stability of the international monetary system, which the IMF plays a principal role in safeguarding.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I would also like to add, Mr Speaker, that the IMF's mandate and functions continue to receive broad support from across its 191 member countries, including that of its larger members.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Saktiandi also asked how the Government decides which organisations or international efforts to support.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The Government assesses each organisation on its merits.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Saktiandi and Mr Ng Shi Xuan both asked how Singapore's contributions compare to other countries.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The US and Japan have pledged to contribute to the PRG-HIPC as well.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In our region, other than our ASEAN counterparts, China and Korea have also pledged contributions.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim asked how the amounts are ascertained.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It is a point I made earlier on.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: These quota shares are determined by a country's relative position in the global economy, using a set of indicators comprising GDP, openness, economic variability and international reserves.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Naturally, countries with larger quota shares are expected to contribute more.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Assoc Prof Lim also asked whether our earlier contributions had been drawn down.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Saktiandi also asked about the PRGT's self-sustainability.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The IMF aims for the PRGT to be financially self-sustainable in the long run.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In recent years, this has been challenging as overall demand for PRGT funding remained higher compared to demand pre-pandemic.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This round of contributions is targeted at getting the PRGT closer to its goal of self-sustainability.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The IMF has also approved a comprehensive package of policy reforms and financing measures.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: These reforms naturally need time to implement and to be assessed for its efficacy.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This is to ensure that the PRGT's long-term self-sustainability may be reached.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: On a related note, Mr Ng Shi Xuan and Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked about future IMF grant requests.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: IMF's fundraising requests are informed by periodic assessments of the demand for its various facilities and initiatives.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This in turn rests on the state of the global economy and the financial system, and the needs of poor and vulnerable members.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Singapore last contributed to the IMF in 2016 and 2021, which the Members have alluded to, and these were brought to Parliament for approval.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: For any further request for financial assistance, MAS will carefully assess on a case-by-case basis the merits of the request and if the requested amount is reasonable.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: All proposed contributions to the IMF will also be assessed against the conditions under the Bretton Woods Agreements Act.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Saktiandi also asked about the financing and reserves implications of the contributions.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The proposed limit does not include the previous contribution to the PRGT.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We previously contributed 14.5 million SDR to the IMF in 2016, following Parliament's approval.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: On reserves implications, which Members have raised, the proposed amount to the PRGT that will affect our OFR, as I mentioned in my original speech, is negligible relative to the size of MAS' OFR.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The amount should be assessed against the backdrop of the 3.73 billion SDR that Singapore was allocated in the IMF's 2021 SDR General Allocation.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: MAS takes into consideration the contribution request relative to the size of MAS' OFR.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Our past contributions have not impeded MAS in carrying out its mission of ensuring monetary stability, nor do we foresee the current contributions impacting MAS' mission.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Ng Shi Xuan, Mr Victor Lye and Mr Shawn Loh asked about governance and accountability.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The IMF has institutionalised a set of procedures for the use of financing facilities.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: These involve safeguards, oversight and approvals by the IMF Executive Board, which represents the membership of the IMF.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Singapore is represented on the Board through the Southeast Asia Voting Group.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The IMF also imposes conditionalities on members' use of its financing facilities, requiring members to put in place appropriate programmes and implement reforms that will improve their macroeconomic conditions.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The IMF has also a preferred creditor status and borrowing countries are expected to repay the IMF before other creditors.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In addition, IMF regularly updates member countries, including Singapore, on the status and utilisation of our grant contributions.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The IMF had provided debt relief to 38 out of the 39 eligible countries that Assoc Prof Lim had mentioned.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Of which, Sudan is the last country to be eligible under this initiative.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The IMF has a framework for countries to qualify for debt relief under this HIPC initiative.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: For instance, satisfactory performance under the programmes, implementation of the poverty reduction strategy and key structural reforms.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Loh also asked about the mechanism of Singapore's loan to the IMF's RST.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This is included in MAS' media release last Wednesday.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The RST is an IMF-administered loan-based trust to help low-income and vulnerable middle-income countries build resilience to external shocks and to ensure sustainable growth.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It contributes to their longer-term balance of payment stability.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: After this Trust was established in 2022, the IMF sought contributions from 35 member countries with strong external positions, including Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The contributions to the RST are considered loans and other financial assistance under the Bretton Woods Agreements Act, which do not require Parliament's approval.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Shawn Loh rightly pointed out that loans will continue to be recognised as assets on MAS' balance sheet and are not expenses – in contrast to the two grants that we are tabling today.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Loh also asked about the risks associated with this contribution.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: When Singapore provides a loan in support of an IMF programme, such as the RST, for the benefit of one or more countries, we are providing the loan to the IMF and entering into an agreement with the IMF.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, we take on the credit risk of the IMF, which is low, instead of the direct credit risk of the countries that the IMF lends to.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As I shared earlier, the IMF has formal procedures for the use of its financing facilities, with safeguards and approvals, and conditionalities on members' use.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As the IMF enjoys preferred creditor status, loans granted by the IMF must be repaid ahead of all other creditors.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The IMF, with the advantage it has from its preferred creditor status and the sizeable reserves it can use to protect its members, has always repaid its own creditors.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In addition, member countries' loans to the IMF under the RST are remunerated at the SDR interest rate.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: To Mr Saktiandi Supaat's question on the loan exposure under the RST, the recent contributions to the RST announced is a once-off.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Any future requests will be similarly carefully considered on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As I highlighted earlier, our considerations will be based on the merits of the request, whether the amount sought is reasonable and, as Mr Saktiandi Supaat mentioned, the implications for our reserves.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Ng also asked about the options Singapore can exercise in the event of budgetary constraints.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I also thank Assoc Prof Jamus Lim's support for these Motions and his call for Singapore to do more.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: He has made this call in previous Sittings.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It is in fact the sentiment that many of us share.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We want to be a force for good in the world.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I think it is heartening that Parliament has expressed that.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Indeed, Singapore has benefited from funding provided by the World Bank in the early years of our infrastructural development, which Mr Saktiandi had mentioned earlier on.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But even as we want to do good, we need to take a balanced approach.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Our resources, as we have articulated many times in this House, are not infinite.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Every dollar we commit abroad must be weighed against our needs at home – for our seniors, for our healthcare and our social safety nets.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As I shared earlier, our contributions to the IMF are fair in that they are pegged to our quota share and assessed to be reasonable.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It does not require Singapore to overextend ourselves even as we do good.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim made a suggestion that he has made previously about institutionalising foreign international assistance.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Our approach first looks at what is commensurate with Singapore's resources, and which best leverages our specific strengths.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Last year in April 2025, the Prime Minister announced the new unit in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, then called the Development Partnership Unit and now the Development Strategy Unit, to coordinate efforts across Government agencies to strengthen coordination and collaboration and focus on areas where Singapore can make a meaningful impact.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We continue to extend capacity building and skills training to developing countries through our Singapore Cooperation Programme (SCP).

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: To date, over 160,000 officials from 180 countries have attended our SCP.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In fact, we are doing more, but in a way that is effective, that makes the best use of our strengths and ultimately, that is in Singapore's best interests.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We had discussed this particular point in the last debate in this House in 2021, as I have explained in my speech earlier.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We will put out additional public communications, such as social media posts and others, on this.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In fact, it is indeed important that Singaporeans appreciate, like Members of this House, the external environment we are in today and how that shapes Singapore's stature and posture in supporting and contributing to relevant multilateral initiatives.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Are there any further clarifications for Minister of State Tan?
